entries.s: Hebrew alphabet reversal (A↔Z). Self-inverse monoalphabetic substitution.
Shift each letter by a fixed amount. Brute-forceable in 25 tries.
Self-inverse Caesar with shift 13. Used to hide spoilers, not for security.
Wrap message around a rod of N rows. Transposition by columnar reading.
5×5 grid maps each letter to a row/column digit pair.
Each plaintext letter maps to one fixed ciphertext letter. Broken by frequency analysis.
Geometric substitution: each letter becomes the lines and dots of its grid cell.
5-bit binary encoding (a/b → letter). Ancestor of ASCII; can hide in typography.
Each letter has multiple ciphertext symbols, flattening frequency.
Rossignol nomenclator mapping numbers to syllables, with traps. Unread for 200 years.
Nomenclator used in Mary Queen of Scots conspiracy. Phelippes added a forged 'doubleth' postscript.
Homophonic substitution with nulls from the 18th-c. Oculist Order manuscript.
Reversible EVA-glyph round-tripper for the unsolved manuscript.
Book cipher using the Declaration of Independence. Two of three remain unsolved.
Homophonic substitution. Z340 cracked in 2020 with diagonal transposition.
CIA HQ sculpture. K1/K2 are keyed Vigenère, K3 columnar transposition, K4 still open.
Words encoded as page/line/word triplets in a shared book.
Polybius numbers added (mod 100) to keyword Polybius numbers.
Common letters get one digit, rare letters two — variable-length code.
KGB hand cipher: straddling checkerboard + double transposition + date keystream.
Hand stream cipher driven by a 54-card deck. Featured in Cryptonomicon.
Rotating cipher disk; first true polyalphabetic substitution.
Polyalphabetic shift driven by a repeating keyword. 'Le chiffre indéchiffrable.'
Reciprocal Vigenère variant — encryption equals decryption.
13-row reciprocal table; each key letter swaps two halves of the alphabet.
Vigenère with numeric keys 0–9. Smaller key space.
Vigenère using a long natural-language passage as the key.
Standard Vigenère with three Confederate keywords ('Manchester Bluff', 'Complete Victory', 'Come Retribution').
Zig-zag transposition on N rails.
Plaintext into rows under a keyword, then read columns out in keyword order.
Two keyed columnar transpositions. WWII workhorse; broken by modern hill-climbing.
Polybius with letters A/D/F/G/X then keyed columnar transposition.
36-character ADFGX upgrade adding digits. Painvin broke it under deadline.
Polybius coordinates split, transposed across a period, then recombined.
3D Polybius (3×3×3 cube) — fractionates into trits and shuffles.
Two keyed squares plus two standard ones — disrupts digram frequencies.
Lighter Delastelle variant with two squares (horizontal or vertical orientation).
Digram cipher on a keyed 5×5 square. British Boer War & WWI use.
Text → Morse → regroup dots/dashes/separators in trigrams → keyed substitution.
Polybius substitution + numeric-keyword transposition.
Multiplies plaintext blocks by an invertible matrix mod 26. First mathematical cipher.
Union route cipher: transpose whole words, salt with code names.

entries.b: Reused as M-94 (1922) and broken late 20th c.
entries.s: 26-disk wheel cipher. Line up plaintext on one row, read ciphertext from another.
Six co-prime pin-wheels and a 27-bar lug cage producing a Beaufort shift per character.
Three-rotor Wehrmacht Enigma with plugboard, reflector, and stepping.
Two 26-letter alphabets that permute themselves after every character.
XOR stream cipher with two sets of pin-wheels. Colossus was built to break it.
Japanese diplomatic stepping-switch cipher. Broken without ever seeing the machine.
XOR of plaintext with a key tape — original teleprinter stream cipher.
Truly random key the same length as the message. Provably unbreakable when used correctly.
5×5 Polybius tapped as row-then-column knocks. Used by POWs in Vietnam.
WWII Navajo military vocabulary code (e.g. 'iron fish' = submarine).
Vigenère's self-extending key — the message itself becomes the key after the keyword is exhausted.
Substitution alphabet plus a 1,000-2,000 entry codebook of words and names. The 400-year diplomatic standard.
If both correspondents share a book, the book itself is the key. Used by Benedict Arnold, Aaron Burr, Beale, SOE.
Edward Elgar's 87-character cryptogram to Dora Penny. Unbroken in 125+ years of attempts.
American WWII strategic rotor machine — 15 rotors with pseudo-random stepping. Never broken by the Axis.
British improved Enigma — 5 rotors, no plugboard, multi-notch stepping. Bletchley used Typex to emulate Enigma.
First public government-standardised cipher; 16-round Feistel, 56-bit key. Birthed academic cryptanalysis.
Two strangers create a shared secret over an open wire. The protocol that ended must-meet-first cryptography.
First practical public-key cryptosystem. Encrypt with one key, decrypt with another. TLS, code signing, PGP.
The cipher that encrypts the modern world. Substitution-permutation network, 128-bit blocks, 10–14 rounds.
256-bit fingerprint for any input. The verification engine of Git, Bitcoin, TLS certificates, software integrity.
Scytale, Atbash, Caesar, ROT13, Polybius — the founding ciphers.
Monoalphabetic, Pigpen, Bacon, Homophonic, Playfair, Hill, Bifid, Trifid, Four/Two-Square, Fractionated Morse.
Alberti, Vigenère, Beaufort, Porta, Gronsfeld, Running Key, Bazeries.
Rail Fence, Columnar, Double Transposition.
Babington, Stager, Confederate Vigenère, Dictionary Code, Nihilist, ADFGX/ADFGVX, Straddling Checkerboard, VIC, Tap Code, Navajo.
Jefferson Disk, Enigma, Lorenz, M-209, Chaocipher, Purple.
Voynich, Great Cipher, Babington, Copiale, Beale, Zodiac, Kryptos.

21 stories: Al-Kindi, Phelippes, Babbage/Kasiski, Painvin, Friedman, Rejewski, Turing, Tutte, Hagelin, Rowlett, Grotjan, Knight team, Rubin/Lasry, Zodiac team, Bazeries, Clarke, Tutte (solo), Elizebeth Friedman, Driscoll, Marks.
Five primitives that replaced classical cryptography: DES, Diffie-Hellman, RSA, AES, SHA-256. Mathematical hardness, public-key, and key sizes large enough that brute force is physically impossible.
Vernam, One-Time Pad, Solitaire — provable security and the limits of secrecy.
Stager, Confederate Vigenère, dictionary codes, telegraphic warfare.
Interactive 2,500-year timeline with era filtering and clickable events.
Architectural floor plan of all halls + complete cipher index.
Sortable, filterable comparison of all 52 ciphers.
Visual relationship map between cipher families.
10 interactive techniques: frequency, Kasiski, IoC, crib dragging, hill climbing, simulated annealing, stepping-switch, HMM/SMT, chaocipher reconstruction.
10 progressive cracking puzzles from Caesar to Enigma.
Encrypt, decrypt, and analyze across many ciphers in one tool.
Cryptography term reference.
From Shannon to AES, RSA, elliptic curves, and post-quantum.
Guided pathway through cipher concepts.
Themed tours: Wartime, Mathematics, Hacker.
Discussion space for cipher enthusiasts.
Ancient Indian substitution cipher from the Kama Sutra — pairing letters for secret communication.
Early hieroglyphic substitution inscriptions — the first known deliberate cipher-like transformation in history.
Greek military cipher described by Aeneas Tacticus — holes in a wound disk encode letters.
Medieval Islamic cipher techniques from al-Kindi and the House of Wisdom — first cryptanalysts.
The trilingual decree that unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphics — the key to the most famous decipherment in history.
Herodotus's account of a secret message tattooed on a shaved head — the oldest recorded act of steganography.
A fired clay disc from Minoan Crete bearing undeciphered spiral text — one of the oldest potential cipher texts.
Eight mysterious letters carved beneath a Shepherd's Monument in Staffordshire — possibly a Templar or Masonic code.
A cipher included in Codes and Ciphers (1939) that the author later admitted he'd forgotten how to decode.
An unidentified dead man found on an Australian beach with a torn scrap reading "Tamam Shud" — the code page beside him remains unsolved.
Papers found on the body of Ricky McCormick contain two pages of undeciphered cipher text — open FBI cold case.
The main Imperial Japanese Navy operational cipher — broken by Station HYPO to win the Battle of Midway.
The Red machine — Japan's pre-war diplomatic cipher broken by William Friedman's team in 1936.
Soviet 10-rotor cipher machine used by Warsaw Pact — considered the Soviet counterpart to SIGABA.
US/NATO rotor cipher machine — whose keys were sold to the KGB by John Walker for 18 years.
German Siemens teleprinter cipher machine broken by Swedish mathematician Arne Beurling in two weeks.
Elegant German cipher wheel machine that William Friedman broke in 2.5 hours — a masterclass in cryptanalysis.
US Army strip cipher device based on Jefferson Disk design — standard equipment from WWI through WWII.
Extended Caesar using a linear function ax+b (mod 26) — generalizes shift ciphers with multiplication.
Johannes Trithemius's progressive cipher — an early polyalphabetic system predating Vigenère by 50 years.
Autokey variant attributed to Girolamo Cardano — uses the plaintext itself as a running key.
Charles Wheatstone's double-substitution cipher using a 5×5 grid — closely related to Playfair.
International encoding system using dots and dashes — historically confused with encryption but actually a public code.
Null cipher using a perforated mask — only the letters through the holes are the message.
Messages hidden by making most of the text meaningless — the message is encoded in selected letters.
Papal nomenclator system used by the Vatican Secret Archives — among the most sophisticated Renaissance ciphers.
John Wallis's seventeenth-century frequency analysis methods applied to Royalist ciphers.
Four-digit codebook system to transmit Chinese characters over telegraph — the world's longest-used commercial code.
The intercepted German diplomatic telegram that brought America into WWI — decoded by British Room 40.
British tactical field cipher using sliding card grid — fast and portable, used in WWII field operations.
Victorian-era codebooks for compressing and concealing cable telegrams — the business predecessor of encryption.
George Washington's Revolutionary War spy network using invisible ink and numbered codebooks — America's first signals intelligence.
The Ottendorf cipher used by Benedict Arnold and John André — America's most famous act of treason encoded in a book cipher.
J.S. Bach's hidden musical signatures — B-A-C-H in German musical notation and numerological patterns in his compositions.
Holmes's fictional stick-figure substitution cipher from The Adventure of the Dancing Men — actually a monoalphabetic substitution.
Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 story featuring a frequency-analysis attack on a substitution cipher — the first popular cryptanalysis narrative.
The most elaborate ARG cipher puzzle in history — using steganography, OTP, Liber Primus, and PGP across global physical locations.
Online alternate-reality game cipher challenges that pioneered the ARG genre and community puzzle-solving methodology.
The MIT Mystery Hunt — the world's oldest and most complex competitive puzzle hunt, featuring novel cipher designs since 1980.
A 2,000-year-old Latin palindrome word square found across the Roman Empire — SATOR AREPO TENET OPERA ROTAS.
The Freemason cipher using geometric grid shapes to encode letters — widely documented and culturally significant.
US Army field one-time pad system — the operational standard for covert communication during the Cold War.
Che Guevara's use of VIC cipher variants for Latin American guerrilla communications — documented in his diary.
The Provisional IRA's operational codebook system — book cipher variants for covert communication.
One-time pad communications used by the German Red Army Faction terrorist organization.
Viet Minh and NLF substitution cipher systems used during the First and Second Indochina Wars.

entries.s: Classical Korean diplomatic cipher system used by Joseon dynasty administrators and couriers.

entries.h: Hall I: World Origins of Cryptography
entries.s: Ethiopian ecclesiastical cipher traditions using the Ge'ez script — monastic cryptography from the Ethiopian highlands.
Commercial and diplomatic codebooks used across Latin America — from Buenos Aires telegraph codes to Mexican diplomatic cipher.
Coded communication in African American field hollers and spirituals — linguistic steganography under slavery.
Dan Brown's thriller that introduced 80 million readers to Atbash and cryptographic thinking.
Disney film featuring Freemason ciphers, founding-era American codes, and cipher-hunt tourism.
Disney animated series that hid Caesar, Atbash, and Vigenère ciphers in episode credits — teaching real cryptography to children.
Spy technique reducing a full page of text to a dot the size of a period — the most effective Cold War covert communication tool.
European state mail interception bureaux — the original signals intelligence agencies.
US Navy codebreaking unit at Pearl Harbor that broke JN-25 and won the Battle of Midway.
Britain's WWII codebreaking headquarters — where 10,000 people broke Enigma, Lorenz, and invented Colossus.
Auguste Kerckhoffs's 1883 rule — security must depend on key secrecy alone, not algorithm secrecy.
Cold War US SIGINT operation that broke Soviet OTP traffic by exploiting key reuse — revealing the Rosenbergs and Cambridge Five.
Bell Labs voice OTP system — the world's first secure speech encryption, protecting Churchill-Roosevelt phone calls.
US Navy commander who led Station HYPO and broke JN-25 to win the Battle of Midway.
Swedish mathematician who broke the Geheimschreiber cipher solo in two weeks — perhaps the greatest individual cryptanalytic feat.
British cryptanalyst who first reconstructed Enigma wiring and broke the Abwehr Enigma at Bletchley.
Founder of America's Black Chamber — broke Japanese codes at the Washington Naval Conference, then published everything.
Bletchley Park cryptanalyst who broke Italian naval Enigma at age 19, enabling the Battle of Cape Matapan.
GCHQ mathematicians who invented public-key cryptography in 1970–73 — classified until 1997 while RSA received public credit.
Author of The Codebreakers — the first comprehensive history of cryptography, which the NSA tried to suppress.
Game designer and cryptographer — curator of the Famous Unsolved Codes list and foremost Kryptos K4 researcher.
Computational cryptanalyst who solved the Copiale Cipher and contributed to the Zodiac Z340 solution.
Hall of mysteries — cryptographic puzzles from the ancient world to the present day that remain unsolved.
Cipher in culture — the presence and influence of cryptography in art, literature, film, games, and music.
US Navy cryptanalyst — "Madame X" — who broke Japanese naval codes between the world wars and trained a generation of US codebreakers.
Bletchley Park cryptanalyst who reverse-engineered the Lorenz SZ40 cipher machine from ciphertext alone — one of the greatest cryptanalytic feats in history.
Pioneering US codebreaker who broke Prohibition-era smuggling codes and Nazi spy ring ciphers in South America for the Coast Guard and FBI.
Bletchley Park cryptanalyst in Hut 8 who worked alongside Alan Turing on Naval Enigma — one of the few women promoted to senior cryptanalyst rank.
SOE cryptographer who designed silk one-time-pad codes for agents in occupied Europe and authored the poem-code memoir Between Silk and Cyanide.
US Army strip cipher device based on Jefferson Disk design — standard equipment from WWI through WWII.
57 enciphered letters from Mary, Queen of Scots to Michel de Castelnau, decoded in 2023 by Lasry, Biermann, and Tomokiyo using hill-climbing on a homophonic nomenclator.
International encoding system using dots and dashes — historically confused with encryption but actually a public code.
Robert Patterson's columnar transposition with line-shuffling and random null padding, sent to Thomas Jefferson and unsolved until George Lasry broke it in 2009.
ELS claims to find hidden prophecies in the Hebrew Bible. McKay et al. (1999) showed the same method produces identical results in War and Peace and Moby-Dick.
Paste unknown ciphertext and let the Cipher Detective walk you through frequency analysis, Index of Coincidence, and Kasiski examination to identify the most likely cipher family.
100,026 verified ciphertext records across 82 cipher types, 84 engines, and 9 languages. Known-answer benchmark dataset for learning, teaching, and cryptanalysis tool evaluation.
